entry.title: Understanding Virtualization and Hypervisors: A Technical Introduction

link.title: Understanding Virtualization and Hypervisors: A Technical Introduction

entry.content:
Virtualization is a foundational concept in modern computing, allowing multiple isolated operating systems to share the same physical hardware.
It underpins cloud computing, data center scalability, and secure workload isolation.

This post provides a technically rich yet accessible introduction to virtualization, its architecture, and the different types of hypervisors, with clickable academic and industry references.

1. What Is Virtualization?

At its core, virtualization is the process of abstracting hardware resources — such as CPU, memory, storage, and network — into virtual resources that multiple virtual machines (VMs) can use simultaneously.

Each VM behaves as though it has its own hardware, thanks to a layer called the hypervisor (or Virtual Machine Monitor, VMM).

+——————————————————-+ | Virtual Machines (VMs) | | +———+ +———+ +———+ | | | GuestOS | | GuestOS | | GuestOS | | | +———+ +———+ +———+ | | | Virtual Hardware (vCPU, vRAM, vNIC) | | +——————————————————-+ | Hypervisor (VMM Layer) | +——————————————————-+ | Physical Hardware (Host) | +——————————————————-+

In simple terms: virtualization allows one computer to act like many.

2. Why Virtualization Matters

Virtualization provides several critical benefits:

  • Resource Efficiency: Better hardware utilization and consolidation.
  • Isolation: Faults in one VM don’t affect others.
  • Flexibility: Rapid provisioning and scaling.
  • Portability: Live migration and snapshots for fault tolerance.

These capabilities are fundamental to modern clouds such as AWS EC2, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

3. Virtualization Architecture

Here’s a conceptual diagram of how virtualization layers interact:

Figure 1 — The virtualization stack: physical hardware, hypervisor, and guest operating systems (Image source: Medium / VirtuallyGenius).

Layers:

  1. Host Hardware — The actual CPU, memory, I/O, and storage.
  2. Hypervisor — Software that manages VMs and resource scheduling.
  3. Guest OS — Each VM’s operating system (Linux, Windows, etc.).
  4. Applications — User-level processes within each guest.

4. How Virtualization Works

When a guest OS executes privileged CPU instructions, the hypervisor intercepts them and safely emulates or forwards them to the hardware using virtualization extensions.

CPU Vendor Virtualization Extension Notable Features
Intel VT-x (VMX) Hardware-assisted virtualization, EPT for memory mapping
AMD AMD-V (SVM) Nested paging, secure encrypted virtualization
ARM ARM Virtualization Extensions Dedicated EL2 privilege level for hypervisors

CPU Privilege Rings

CPUs traditionally use privilege rings (Ring 0 = kernel, Ring 3 = user space).
Virtualization introduces Ring -1, a special privilege mode for hypervisors:

Ring -1 – Hypervisor (VMM) Ring 0 – Guest OS Kernel Ring 3 – Guest Applications

This ensures hypervisors can manage VMs securely without violating isolation boundaries.

5. Types of Hypervisors

Hypervisors are categorized into Type 1 (bare-metal) and Type 2 (hosted) architectures.

Type 1 — Bare-Metal Hypervisors

Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware, managing guest OSes natively without an intermediary host OS.

Examples:

  • VMware ESXi
  • Microsoft Hyper-V Server
  • Xen Project
  • KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine)

Figure 2 — Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor directly managing guest OSes (Image source: Medium / CloudComputingSimplified).

Key Characteristics:

  • Highest performance and lowest overhead.
  • Preferred for enterprise, data centers, and cloud environments.
  • Direct access to CPU virtualization instructions (VT-x, AMD-V).

Type 2 — Hosted Hypervisors

Type 2 hypervisors run on top of a host OS.
They rely on the host OS for hardware drivers and system management.

Examples:

  • VMware Workstation
  • Oracle VirtualBox
  • Parallels Desktop

Figure 3 — Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor architecture (Image source: Medium / TechWithShubham).

Key Characteristics:

  • Easier to install and use.
  • Slightly higher overhead due to double scheduling (host + guest).
  • Common for testing, development, and education setups.

6. Advanced Virtualization Techniques

Modern hypervisors use several optimization and isolation models:

  • Paravirtualization: Guest OS modified to be “hypervisor-aware” (e.g., Xen PV).
  • Hardware-Assisted Virtualization: Uses CPU extensions to eliminate trapping overhead.
  • Microkernel Hypervisors: Minimal trusted code base, e.g. seL4 and Nova.
  • Nested Virtualization: Running a hypervisor inside another VM — common in research and cloud testbeds.

7. Virtualization vs Containers

Virtualization replicates hardware, while containers virtualize the operating system.

Feature Virtual Machines Containers
Kernel Separate per VM Shared host kernel
Isolation Strong (hardware) Moderate (namespaces)
Startup Time Seconds Milliseconds
Overhead High Low
Example Tools VMware, KVM, Xen Docker, Kubernetes

Figure 4 — Virtual machines vs containers (Image source: Docker Blog).

8. Security Considerations

The hypervisor is part of the system’s Trusted Computing Base (TCB), meaning it must be highly secure and minimal.

Security mechanisms include:

  • IOMMU — Protects against DMA attacks.
  • AMD SEV — Encrypts VM memory for confidentiality.
  • Intel TDX — Isolates VMs in trusted execution domains.
  • Secure Boot — Ensures only verified hypervisors load at startup.

9. Summary Table

Feature Type 1 Hypervisor Type 2 Hypervisor
Execution Environment Bare metal Host OS
Performance High Moderate
Security Strong isolation Depends on host
Example Use Cloud, servers Desktop, testing
Examples KVM, Xen, ESXi VirtualBox, Parallels

References

  1. Popek, G. J., & Goldberg, R. P. (1974). Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures. Communications of the ACM, 17(7), 412–421.
  2. Intel Corporation. Intel® 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer’s Manual. Volume 3, 2023.
  3. AMD. AMD-V™ Architecture Reference Manual., 2022.
  4. Barham, P. et al. Xen and the Art of Virtualization. SOSP, 2003.
  5. Rosenblum, M., & Garfinkel, T. Virtual Machine Monitors: Current Technology and Future Trends. IEEE Computer, 38(5), 2005.
  6. Kivity, A. KVM: The Linux Virtual Machine Monitor. Ottawa Linux Symposium, 2007.
  7. ARM Ltd. Virtualization Extensions Architecture Reference Manual., 2023.

Authored by Luc MAHOP, Ph.D. Student in Computer Science.
Published on https://alshedivat.github.io/blog/2025/virtualization-and-hypervisors

entry.title: A Technical Comparison of x86 and ARM Architectures

link.title: A Technical Comparison of x86 and ARM Architectures

entry.content:
If you’ve ever wondered why your laptop’s Intel processor differs fundamentally from your smartphone’s processor, or why Apple’s M-series chips are so efficient, you’re about to find out. The world of computing is dominated by two processor architectures: x86 (found in most PCs) and ARM (powering smartphones, tablets, and increasingly, laptops and servers). This article explores what makes them different, why it matters, and where each excels.

1. Introduction: Why Processor Architecture Matters

When you run a program on your computer, the processor (CPU) executes a series of instructions. The instruction set architecture (ISA) defines what instructions the processor understands—it’s like the vocabulary and grammar the CPU speaks.

Two families of instruction sets dominate modern computing:

  • x86: Used by Intel and AMD processors in most desktop and laptop computers
  • ARM: Used in virtually all smartphones, tablets, and increasingly in laptops (Apple M-series) and cloud servers (AWS Graviton)

Understanding these architectures helps you make informed decisions about hardware purchases, appreciate performance differences, and understand the technical evolution of computing.

2. The Philosophy Divide: CISC vs RISC

x86: The Complex Instruction Set (CISC)

Think of x86 as a language with a huge vocabulary—over 1,500 different instructions that the processor can understand . The x86 architecture, dating back to Intel’s 8086 processor in 1978, follows the CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computing) philosophy.

Key characteristics:

  • Variable-length instructions: Instructions can be 1 to 15 bytes long . This is like having words of different lengths—some short, some very long.
  • Rich instruction set: Single instructions can do complex operations. For example, one instruction might “load data from memory, multiply it, and store the result” all at once.
  • Backward compatibility: Modern x86 processors can still run software written in the 1980s—an amazing feat, but one that adds complexity .
  • Extensions over time: SSE, AVX, AVX-512 for multimedia and scientific computing .

The trade-off: More powerful instructions mean more complex hardware to decode and execute them. Modern x86 processors actually break down complex instructions into simpler micro-operations (µops) internally—essentially converting CISC to RISC under the hood!

ARM: The Reduced Instruction Set (RISC)

ARM takes the opposite approach: a smaller, simpler vocabulary where each “word” does just one thing, but does it efficiently. ARM (Advanced RISC Machines) was designed in 1985 with simplicity and efficiency in mind .

Key characteristics:

  • Fixed-length instructions: Most instructions are exactly 32 bits (or 16 bits in compact “Thumb” mode) . Like a language where every word is the same length—easier to process.
  • Load-store architecture: Only specific instructions can access memory; arithmetic happens only on data already loaded into registers .
  • Simpler design: Fewer instructions mean simpler hardware, which translates to lower power consumption .
  • Conditional execution: Instructions can be executed conditionally without branching, reducing pipeline stalls .

The trade-off: You might need several ARM instructions to do what one x86 instruction can do, but each ARM instruction executes faster and uses less power.

Visual Comparison

x86 CISC Approach:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Complex Instruction            │
│  "Load, Multiply, Store"        │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓
    [Complex Decoder]
         ↓
    Multiple µops → Execution

ARM RISC Approach:
┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
│  Load    │  │ Multiply │  │  Store   │
└──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
     ↓             ↓             ↓
  [Simple Decoder] → Direct Execution

3. How They Work Under the Hood

While ISA defines what instructions exist, microarchitecture defines how they’re executed. Both x86 and ARM use sophisticated techniques, but with different approaches.

Key Microarchitectural Features Compared

Feature x86 (Intel Core, AMD Zen) ARM (Cortex-A, Apple Silicon)
ISA Type CISC RISC
Pipeline Depth 14–19 stages 9–11 stages
Decode Width 4–6 µops 4–8 instructions
Execution Out-of-order superscalar Out-of-order superscalar
Branch Prediction TAGE hybrid + indirect predictor Neural + perceptron predictors
Cache Design Typically inclusive Often exclusive
Typical Power 45W–125W (laptops/desktops) 5W–20W (phones/laptops)

What this means in practice:

  • Pipeline depth: Think of it as an assembly line. x86’s deeper pipeline can process more instructions simultaneously but is harder to keep full and wastes more energy when predictions are wrong .
  • Out-of-order execution: Both architectures execute instructions out of order when safe to do so, maximizing efficiency. Modern ARM processors are just as sophisticated as x86 in this regard .
  • Branch prediction: Both use advanced techniques to guess which way a program will branch, keeping the pipeline full. Apple’s M-series chips use neural network-based predictors—cutting-edge technology .

Example: Adding Two Numbers

x86 approach:

add eax, [memory_address]  ; One instruction: load from memory and add

ARM approach:

ldr r0, [memory_address]   ; Load from memory into register
add r1, r1, r0             ; Add registers

ARM uses two instructions, but each is simpler and executes faster. The total time and energy can be less due to the simpler hardware .

4. Power and Efficiency: The Great Divide

This is where ARM truly shines and why it dominates mobile computing.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Let’s compare two high-performance processors:

Metric Intel Core i9-13900K (x86) Apple M2 (ARM)
Peak Power 125W 20W
Performance per Watt 1× (baseline) ~4.5× better
Core Count 24 cores (8P + 16E) 8 cores (4P + 4E)
Manufacturing Process Intel 7 (10nm Enhanced) TSMC 5nm
Use Case Desktop PCs, workstations Laptops, tablets

What this means: The M2 delivers similar single-threaded performance while consuming approximately 1/6th the power . This is why MacBooks can run for 15-20 hours on battery while Windows laptops struggle to reach 8 hours .

Why ARM is More Efficient

  1. Simpler instruction decoding: Less energy spent figuring out what instructions mean
  2. Shallower pipelines: Less work wasted when predictions are wrong
  3. SoC integration: Memory, CPU, and GPU on one chip reduces power-hungry data transfers
  4. Optimized for efficiency: ARM designs prioritize performance-per-watt from the start

Why x86 Uses More Power

  1. Legacy compatibility: Supporting decades-old instructions adds overhead
  2. Complex decoding: Breaking CISC into µops requires more transistors and power
  3. Deeper speculation: More aggressive predictions mean more wasted work when wrong
  4. Discrete components: Traditional PC designs with separate CPU, chipset, and memory

The Hybrid Core Revolution

Both architectures now use hybrid designs mixing Performance (P) and Efficiency (E) cores :

Modern Hybrid CPU Design:
┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Performance Cores (P-cores)       │
│  • Higher frequency                │
│  • More complex                    │
│  • For demanding tasks             │
├────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Efficiency Cores (E-cores)        │
│  • Lower frequency                 │
│  • Simpler design                  │
│  • For background tasks            │
└────────────────────────────────────┘

This approach, pioneered by ARM’s big.LITTLE in 2011 and perfected by Apple’s M-series , is now standard in Intel’s 12th gen+ processors .

5. Software and Compatibility

Having the best hardware means nothing without software. Let’s see how both ecosystems compare.

x86 Software Ecosystem

Strengths:

  • Maturity: 40+ years of software development
  • Compatibility: Run Windows software from the 1990s on modern processors
  • Developer tools: Highly optimized compilers (GCC, LLVM, Visual Studio)
  • Enterprise software: Most business applications target x86
  • Gaming: DirectX and most games are optimized for x86

Presence:

  • Windows (dominant)
  • Linux servers and desktops
  • macOS (until 2020)
  • High-performance computing (HPC)

ARM Software Ecosystem

Strengths:

  • Mobile dominance: 100% of smartphones use ARM
  • Energy efficiency: Perfect for battery-powered devices
  • Growing server presence: AWS Graviton, Ampere Altra in cloud computing
  • Modern development: Native support in latest tools and languages

Presence:

  • All Android devices (3+ billion active)
  • All iOS devices (1.5+ billion active)
  • Apple Silicon Macs (M1, M2, M3)
  • Many embedded systems
  • Supercomputers: Fugaku (world’s fastest in 2020)

The Compatibility Challenge

When Apple switched from x86 (Intel) to ARM (Apple Silicon) in 2020 , they faced a huge challenge: how to run existing x86 Mac apps?

Solution: Rosetta 2

  • Translates x86 code to ARM on-the-fly
  • Most apps run at 70-80% of native speed—still very fast!
  • Users barely notice they’re running translated code

Similar efforts:

  • Windows on ARM: Microsoft’s x86/x64 emulation
  • QEMU: Open-source emulation for Linux
  • Box86/Box64: x86 emulation on ARM Linux

Developer Perspective

Modern development often doesn’t care about architecture:

High-Level Code (Python, JavaScript, Java)
              ↓
    [Compiler/Interpreter]
              ↓
    Architecture-Specific Code
         ↙         ↘
      x86        ARM

Languages like Python, JavaScript, and Java are architecture-independent—the interpreter handles the differences . This is why ARM’s rise has been relatively smooth.

6. Security Features Compared

Both architectures have evolved sophisticated security features, though with different approaches.

Security Feature Comparison

Security Feature x86 ARM
Virtualization Support Intel VT-x, AMD-V ARM Virtualization Extensions
Secure Enclaves Intel SGX TrustZone
Memory Protection CET MTE
Pointer Security Limited PAC
Secure Boot UEFI Secure Boot ARM Trusted Boot
Encrypted VMs AMD SEV, Intel TDX TrustZone, Realm Management

Understanding Key Security Features

Intel SGX (x86)

  • Creates protected memory regions called “enclaves”
  • Even the operating system can’t peek inside
  • Great for cloud computing: run sensitive code on untrusted servers

ARM TrustZone

  • Splits the processor into two worlds: Secure and Normal
  • Like having two computers in one chip
  • Used for payment processing, DRM, biometric authentication on phones

Memory Tagging (ARM MTE)

  • Assigns “tags” to memory regions
  • Catches buffer overflows and use-after-free bugs
  • Built into ARMv8.5-A and newer

Pointer Authentication (ARM PAC)

  • Cryptographically signs pointers
  • Prevents attackers from redirecting program execution
  • Makes exploits much harder

Why This Matters

  • Mobile devices: ARM’s TrustZone secures fingerprint data, payment info
  • Cloud computing: x86’s SEV enables confidential computing
  • IoT devices: ARM’s security features protect smart home devices
  • Financial systems: Both architectures support hardware-backed security

7. Real-World Performance Benchmarks

Let’s look at how these architectures perform in practice.

Single-Core Performance

Modern ARM processors have caught up to x86 in single-threaded performance :

Benchmark Intel i9-13900K Apple M2 Pro AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
Geekbench 6 (Single) ~2,200 ~2,650 ~2,300
Cinebench R23 (Single) ~2,200 ~1,580 ~2,000
Power Draw (Single Core) ~25W ~5W ~22W

Key insight: Apple’s M2 matches or exceeds x86 single-core performance while using 1/5th the power .

Multi-Core Performance

x86 still holds advantages in raw multi-core throughput :

Benchmark Intel i9-13900K (24 cores) Apple M2 Max (12 cores) AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (16 cores)
Geekbench 6 (Multi) ~24,000 ~14,000 ~23,000
Cinebench R23 (Multi) ~40,000 ~14,000 ~38,000
Power Draw (Full Load) ~250W ~40W ~230W

Key insight: More cores help x86, but the power consumption difference is dramatic .

Performance Per Watt (The Key Metric)

When we account for power consumption :

Performance Per Watt Rankings (Normalized):
1. Apple M2 (ARM)      ████████████████████ 100%
2. Apple M1 (ARM)      ████████████████░░░░  85%
3. AMD Ryzen 7950X     █████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  25%
4. Intel i9-13900K     ████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  22%

Real-World Scenarios

Video Encoding (HandBrake) :

  • Intel i9-13900K: Fast (8 minutes), Hot (95°C), Loud fans
  • Apple M2 Pro: Nearly as fast (10 minutes), Cool (60°C), Silent
  • Winner: ARM for laptops, x86 for desktop power users

Gaming (1080p) :

  • x86 with dedicated GPU: 150+ FPS in AAA games
  • Apple M2 Pro: 60-80 FPS in compatible games
  • Winner: x86 (but limited by game support, not architecture)

Battery Life (13” Laptop) :

  • x86 laptop: 4-8 hours typical
  • ARM laptop (M2 MacBook): 15-20 hours
  • Winner: ARM, dramatically

Software Development (Compiling large projects) :

  • Modern compilers optimized for both
  • Performance roughly equivalent when core counts match
  • Winner: Tie (both excellent)

8. The Future of Both Architectures

Both x86 and ARM continue to evolve, and their futures are surprisingly intertwined.

x86’s Evolution

Intel’s Plans:

  • Intel 4 and Intel 3 processes: Catching up to TSMC in chip manufacturing
  • Hybrid architecture expansion: More efficient E-cores
  • AI acceleration: Built-in AI engines (Lunar Lake, Arrow Lake)
  • APX (Advanced Performance Extensions): New instructions for better performance

AMD’s Plans:

  • Zen 5 architecture: Further IPC improvements
  • 3D V-Cache expansion: More cache for gaming and HPC
  • XDNA AI engines: Competing with Intel in AI acceleration
  • Improved power efficiency: Learning from ARM’s success

ARM’s Evolution

ARM v9 and Beyond :

  • Scalable Vector Extension 2 (SVE2): Better for scientific computing
  • Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA): Enhanced security for cloud
  • Performance improvements: Closing gap with x86 in desktop workloads
  • Server market push: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud expanding ARM offerings

Apple’s Trajectory :

  • M3, M4, and beyond: Each generation brings 15-20% improvements
  • Ray tracing acceleration: Catching up to dedicated GPUs
  • AI/ML focus: Neural engines becoming more powerful
  • Desktop replacement: Mac Pro and Mac Studio targeting workstation market

The Rise of RISC-V

A third architecture is emerging: RISC-V, an open-source instruction set .

Why it matters:

  • No licensing fees (unlike ARM)
  • Customizable (add your own instructions)
  • Growing adoption in embedded systems and China

Where it’s going:

  • Low-power devices (IoT, wearables)
  • Academic research
  • Specialized applications
  • Potential challenge to ARM in developing markets

The Convergence Trend

Interestingly, x86 and ARM are becoming more similar :

x86 adopting ARM ideas:

  • Hybrid core designs (P-cores + E-cores)
  • Focus on power efficiency
  • SoC integration
  • Simplified instruction decoding internally

ARM adopting x86 strengths:

  • Wider out-of-order execution
  • More aggressive speculation
  • Larger caches
  • Server-class features (RAS, virtualization) 
The Convergence:
        x86 ←─────────→ ARM
          ↓           ↓
    Hybrid Design, Advanced OoO,
    Power Efficiency, SoC Integration

9. Which Should You Care About?

The answer depends on your needs and use case.

Choose x86 When You Need:

✅ Maximum compatibility

  • Running Windows software, especially legacy apps
  • Gaming with the widest game library
  • Enterprise software that requires x86

✅ Raw computing power

  • Video editing with timeline preview (Adobe Premiere)
  • 3D rendering (Blender, V-Ray)
  • Scientific computing with x86-optimized libraries

✅ Upgradability

  • Desktop PCs you can customize
  • Ability to swap CPUs, RAM, GPUs

✅ Industry-standard servers

  • Running Linux servers with x86-only dependencies
  • Virtual machine hosts with wide guest OS support

Choose ARM When You Need:

✅ Battery life

  • Laptops that last all day (or two days)
  • Tablets and mobile devices
  • Portable workstations

✅ Power efficiency

  • Fanless designs (silent operation)
  • Lower electricity bills for servers
  • Reduced cooling requirements

✅ Modern development

  • Mobile app development (iOS, Android)
  • Cloud-native applications
  • Containerized workloads (Docker, Kubernetes)

✅ Integrated performance

  • Video encoding with dedicated hardware
  • Machine learning on Neural Engines
  • Unified memory architecture

The Reality: It’s Not Binary

Many professionals now use both:

  • Developers: ARM MacBook for portable work, x86 desktop for heavy lifting
  • Cloud architects: ARM instances for cost efficiency , x86 for compatibility
  • Content creators: ARM for on-location, x86 for studio work

The Bottom Line

The “best” architecture depends less on RISC vs CISC philosophy and more on :

  • Microarchitectural implementation quality
  • Manufacturing process technology (5nm, 3nm, etc.)
  • Software optimization
  • Your specific workload and priorities

The truth: Both architectures are excellent. Modern x86 is more efficient than ever, and modern ARM is more powerful than ever. The differences are narrowing, and both will continue to dominate their respective niches while expanding into each other’s territories.

Key Takeaways

  1. x86 (CISC) and ARM (RISC) represent different philosophies, but modern implementations blur the lines
  2. ARM excels in power efficiency (4-5× better performance per watt)
  3. x86 excels in raw performance and backward compatibility
  4. Software ecosystems are maturing for both, with translation layers bridging gaps
  5. Both architectures are converging toward hybrid designs and efficiency
  6. The future is multi-architecture: expect to use both depending on the task

Authored by Luc MAHOP, Ph.D. Student in Computer Science.
Published on https://alshedivat.github.io/blog/2025/x86-vs-arm-architectural-analysis/
entry.summary: Understanding the two dominant processor architectures - a beginner to intermediate guide covering instruction set design, microarchitecture, power efficiency, and real-world performance.

entry.title: The Future of Operating Systems: Current Research Frontiers and Industry Perspectives

link.title: The Future of Operating Systems: Current Research Frontiers and Industry Perspectives

entry.content:
The landscape of operating systems research continues to evolve rapidly, driven by emerging hardware architectures, new application demands, and the persistent quest for better performance, security, and reliability. Recent publications from premier systems conferences like SOSP and OSDI reveal several transformative research directions that are reshaping how we think about OS design. This post explores the main research axes currently driving innovation in operating systems, examining the core problems, recent solutions, and the key industry players investing in these areas.

Formal Verification and Kernel Correctness

Operating system kernels are notoriously difficult to verify due to their complexity and the severe consequences of bugs. The fundamental challenge is ensuring that kernel implementations faithfully follow their specifications while maintaining performance and practical usability. Traditional testing approaches cannot guarantee correctness across all possible execution paths, leaving systems vulnerable to subtle but critical bugs that can compromise security and reliability.

Recent work has made significant strides in practical OS verification. Verus, which won the Distinguished Artifact Award at SOSP 2024, represents a breakthrough in making verification accessible for systems programmers. Built on Rust, Verus provides efficient proof automation that scales to large, complex systems, demonstrating that verified systems code can be both practical and performant. The project has already seen industrial adoption at Microsoft and Amazon, with two of the three best papers at OSDI 2024 built on its foundations. At SOSP 2024, researchers also presented OZZ, a best paper that identifies kernel out-of-order concurrency bugs through in-vivo memory access reordering, addressing a particularly insidious class of kernel bugs that traditional verification methods struggle to catch. The seL4 microkernel project continues to set the gold standard, having achieved the first complete formal verification of a general-purpose OS kernel’s functional correctness from abstract specification down to C implementation as presented in their SOSP 2009 paper. These advances show that formal methods are transitioning from academic curiosities to practical tools that can significantly improve kernel reliability. Microsoft and Amazon are leading industrial efforts in this space, with Google also investing heavily in kernel verification technologies through projects focusing on memory safety and concurrency correctness.

Memory Disaggregation and CXL Integration

Modern datacenters suffer from significant memory stranding, where memory resources remain locally bound to servers even when underutilized, while other nodes experience memory pressure. This rigid coupling between compute and memory leads to poor resource utilization and limits system flexibility. The fundamental problem is enabling efficient access to remote memory with latency and bandwidth characteristics that don’t severely degrade application performance.

Compute Express Link (CXL) technology is revolutionizing how we approach memory disaggregation. At OSDI 2024, researchers from Microsoft presented work on managing memory tiers with CXL in virtualized environments, introducing hardware-managed tiering systems that provide performance close to regular DRAM with minimal degradation for most workloads. Their full-system prototype demonstrated that careful management of memory tiering can maintain application performance while dramatically improving memory utilization across the datacenter. SOSP 2023 featured groundbreaking work on partial failure resilient memory management for CXL-based distributed shared memory, addressing the critical challenge of maintaining system reliability when memory is disaggregated across multiple physical machines. At SOSP 2024, SWARM tackled the problem of replicating shared disaggregated-memory data with minimal overhead, enabling fault-tolerant distributed memory systems that can survive node failures without significant performance penalties. These papers demonstrate that CXL enables a new class of memory architectures where compute and memory resources can be independently scaled and managed. Intel, Microsoft, and Alibaba are at the forefront of CXL-based memory disaggregation, developing both hardware platforms and software stacks to enable this technology in production environments.

eBPF and Programmable Kernel Extensions

Operating system kernels have traditionally been monolithic and difficult to extend, forcing users to choose between kernel modifications (requiring expertise and risking stability) or user-space solutions (sacrificing performance). The core challenge is enabling safe, efficient kernel customization without compromising system security or stability. Users need the ability to extend kernel functionality dynamically for specialized workloads in networking, storage, and observability without the risks associated with traditional kernel modules.

Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) has emerged as a transformative technology for safe kernel programmability. At OSDI 2022, XRP demonstrated how eBPF can be used to implement in-kernel storage functions that achieve speedups close to kernel-bypass solutions while retaining OS integration benefits. By placing eBPF hooks in the NVMe driver’s interrupt handler, XRP enables efficient request chaining for operations like B-tree traversals, dramatically reducing storage access latency. The 2024 ACM SIGCOMM Workshop on eBPF and Kernel Extensions showcased the technology’s rapid evolution, with papers addressing verification challenges, security concerns, and new applications in networking and observability. SafeBPF presented hardware-assisted defense mechanisms to protect against malicious eBPF programs, while other work explored formal verification methods to ensure eBPF program correctness before deployment. These advances demonstrate that eBPF is moving beyond packet filtering to become a general-purpose mechanism for kernel customization, though significant challenges remain in verification, composition, and performance optimization. Meta, Google, and Netflix are heavily invested in eBPF, using it for production-scale networking, load balancing, and observability infrastructure across their massive fleets.

Virtualization and Containerization: Bridging Isolation and Efficiency

Virtualization and containerization technologies form the backbone of modern cloud infrastructure, yet they face an ongoing tension between providing strong isolation guarantees and maintaining operational efficiency. Virtual machines offer complete isolation through hardware virtualization but come with significant overhead in terms of boot time, memory footprint, and inter-VM communication. Containers provide lightweight alternatives with minimal overhead but share the kernel with the host, creating potential security vulnerabilities when running untrusted workloads.

Recent research has focused on narrowing this gap from both directions. At OSDI 2024, researchers presented the HongMeng production microkernel, a commercialized general-purpose microkernel deployed on tens of millions of devices including smartphones, smart routers, and vehicles. HongMeng achieves full Linux API/ABI compatibility while maintaining microkernel security properties through differentiated isolation classes, flexible composition, and address-token-based access control. This work demonstrates that microkernels can be practical for production deployment in diverse scenarios without sacrificing performance. LightVM, presented at SOSP 2017, showed that with careful redesign of the virtualization control plane, VMs can boot in 2.3ms—comparable to Linux fork/exec and orders of magnitude faster than Docker. At the 2024 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing, ConMonitor introduced a lightweight container protection architecture using compact virtualization software to create a trusted computing base that protects container applications from untrusted OS while maintaining efficiency. The 2023 SOSP paper on PVM presented efficient shadow paging for deploying secure containers in cloud-native environments, addressing the fundamental challenge of protecting containers in multi-tenant settings. These innovations show that the traditional tradeoff between isolation and efficiency is not fixed—careful system design can achieve both. VMware, Huawei, and Red Hat are leading industrial development in this space, with VMware focusing on enterprise virtualization optimization, Huawei commercializing microkernel architectures through HongMeng, and Red Hat driving container security innovations through projects like Podman and CRI-O.

Confidential Computing and Trusted Execution Environments

As cloud computing becomes ubiquitous, protecting data in use has emerged as a critical challenge. While encryption at rest and in transit are well-established, data must be decrypted during computation, exposing it to potential attacks from compromised hypervisors, malicious cloud operators, or co-located tenants. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) promise to address this by creating hardware-isolated regions where sensitive code and data can execute securely, but practical deployment faces significant challenges around performance overhead, compatibility, and the evolving threat landscape.

Recent hardware advances and systems research are making confidential computing increasingly practical. Intel’s Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) and AMD’s Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) provide VM-level confidential computing, enabling “lift and shift” deployment of legacy applications with minimal modifications. Honeycomb, presented at OSDI 2023, extended confidential computing to GPUs by securing GPU executions via static validation within AMD SEV-SNP TEE VMs, achieving near-native performance with less than 2% overhead for large language model workloads. This work is particularly significant as GPU-accelerated workloads become central to AI applications. The ASPLOS 2024 paper on VEIL introduced a protected services framework for confidential VMs that enables secure inter-VM communication and resource sharing without exposing sensitive data to the host. A comprehensive empirical analysis comparing Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP revealed critical insights about their performance characteristics, memory management overhead, and I/O inefficiencies that inform practical deployment decisions. However, the recent TEE.Fail attack demonstrated that memory-bus interposition on DDR5 systems can extract secrets from SGX, TDX, and SEV-SNP, highlighting that confidential computing security remains an active research area requiring continued hardware and software co-design. Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA are driving hardware TEE development, while Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS are deploying confidential computing services at scale, with Microsoft and Google leading in integration and attestation services.

Serverless Computing and Cold Start Optimization

Serverless computing promises effortless scaling and pay-per-use economics, but faces a fundamental challenge: cold start latency. When a function hasn’t been invoked recently, the platform must load the function code, initialize the runtime environment, and provision resources before executing the request. For modern workloads, especially those involving large language models, this initialization can take minutes, making serverless impractical for latency-sensitive applications. The problem is compounded by the tension between keeping functions warm (wasting resources during idle periods) and accepting high cold start penalties.

Recent research has tackled this problem from multiple angles. At OSDI 2024, ServerlessLLM introduced a comprehensive solution for serverless LLM inference that reduces cold start latency by 10-200× through three key innovations: fast multi-tier checkpoint loading that efficiently utilizes the entire storage hierarchy on GPU servers, efficient live migration that enables newly initiated inferences to leverage locally cached checkpoints, and startup-time-optimized scheduling that intelligently places models on servers to minimize initialization time. The system demonstrates that even massive models like Llama-70B can be served with acceptable latency in serverless environments. Work presented at OSDI 2023 explored using RDMA-codesigned remote fork mechanisms to eliminate provisioned concurrency requirements, enabling true on-demand function invocation with microsecond-scale startup times. At the 2024 ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing, researchers from multiple institutions examined whether cold starts could be “put in the deep freeze” through predictive prewarming and opportunistic pre-loading strategies that anticipate function invocations before they occur. Another SoCC 2024 paper investigated pre-warming with opportunistic pre-loading to accelerate serverless inference by intelligently caching models based on predicted usage patterns. These approaches show that addressing cold starts requires co-design across the storage system, network infrastructure, and scheduling policies. AWS Lambda, Microsoft Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions are intensively developing cold start mitigation techniques, with each platform offering various keep-warm mechanisms and investing in faster initialization through improved container management and checkpoint loading systems.

Conclusion

Operating systems research continues to address fundamental challenges that directly impact how we build and deploy systems at scale. The convergence of formal verification making kernels more reliable, CXL enabling flexible memory architectures, eBPF providing safe kernel programmability, modern virtualization bridging the isolation-efficiency gap, confidential computing protecting data in use, and serverless optimizations reducing cold start penalties represents a significant evolution in systems design. These are not isolated academic exercises but active areas of industrial investment, with major cloud providers and hardware vendors contributing both to research and production deployment.

As a research scientist working in operating systems and virtualization, I find this era particularly exciting because we’re seeing theoretical advances translate into practical systems deployed at massive scale. The HongMeng microkernel running on tens of millions of devices, CXL memory disaggregation enabling more flexible datacenter architectures, and confidential computing protecting sensitive workloads in public clouds all demonstrate that systems research can have real-world impact. As we look ahead, the integration of these technologies promises operating systems that are simultaneously more reliable, more flexible, more efficient, and better suited to the demands of modern cloud-native and AI-driven workloads. The research community and industry are clearly aligned on these priorities, suggesting that the next generation of operating systems will look markedly different from today’s designs.
entry.summary: The landscape of operating systems research continues to evolve rapidly, driven by emerging hardware architectures, new application demands, and the persistent quest for better performance, security, and reliability. Recent publications from premier systems conferences like SOSP and OSDI reveal several transformative research directions that are reshaping how we think about OS design. This post explores the main research axes currently driving innovation in operating systems, examining the core problems, recent solutions, and the key industry players investing in these areas.
